name: Literally: the strict meaning vs the intensifier
scope: The most-argued-about word in modern English. T1: the strict meaning -- LITERALLY means 'in a literal sense, actually, not figuratively'; 'the pot literally boiled over' means the pot really did boil over (water on the stove). T2: the punchline via misuse -- 'I literally EXPLODED with laughter' -- taken strictly, this means the speaker's body burst apart in the room, which obviously did not happen; it is the FIGURATIVE-intensifier use, the opposite of the strict meaning. T3: the historical surprise -- the intensifier use is not new; writers including Charlotte Bronte (1847), Charles Dickens, and F. Scott Fitzgerald used 'literally' as a figurative intensifier as far back as the early 1800s. Dictionaries including Merriam-Webster now list both senses; the intensifier use is documented for over 200 years. T4: the register call -- in FORMAL writing (essays, news, scientific reporting) use LITERALLY only in its strict sense; in CASUAL speech the intensifier use is understood and standard. Which of these sentences would a good editor flag? T5: the tricky judgment -- 'she was literally the last person to leave' (strict-OK: she really was the last), vs 'he literally died laughing' (intensifier: he did not actually die). Identify which uses the strict sense and which uses the intensifier.
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'literally'; Oxford English Dictionary entry 'literally' (sense 1c, figurative use attested from 1769). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Literally' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Bronte, Dickens, Fitzgerald citations and the Merriam-Webster dual-sense listing. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: verify the 1769 first-attestation date in the OED before writing T3.
framing_note: PRESCRIPTIVE-DESCRIPTIVE FLASHPOINT -- this is the one rung Brandon's bank takes a considered position on: teach the strict meaning as the standard for formal writing, but honestly note the 200-year intensifier history rather than dismissing it as a new degradation. Punchline via misuse: T2 quotes an exploded body. Vocab-teaching at T1 defines LITERALLY inline. Distractor pool: other overused intensifiers ('actually', 'basically', 'totally'), other figures of speech (hyperbole, metaphor).

name: Ironic: not 'unfortunate' and not 'coincidental'
scope: The word most commonly misused in casual speech. T1: the strict meaning -- IRONIC means expressing meaning by using language that signifies the OPPOSITE; saying 'lovely weather!' during a hurricane is verbal irony. T2: the punchline via misuse -- 'It rained on my wedding day -- how ironic!' -- this is UNFORTUNATE, not ironic; rain on a wedding is bad luck, not the opposite of what was said. T3: the Alanis Morissette problem -- her 1995 song 'Ironic' famously lists examples ('rain on your wedding day', 'a free ride when you've already paid') that are mostly coincidence or bad luck, not irony; the song has been used in classrooms for 30 years as a lesson in what irony is NOT. T4: the three main kinds -- VERBAL irony (saying the opposite of what you mean), SITUATIONAL irony (the outcome is the opposite of what was expected -- a fire station burning down), and DRAMATIC irony (the audience knows something the character does not -- Oedipus swearing to find his father's killer). T5: identify which sentence is genuinely ironic and which is merely unfortunate or coincidental -- 'the marriage counselor got divorced' (situational irony -- her job was saving marriages), vs 'I found five dollars the day my paycheck was lost' (coincidence, not irony).
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'ironic, irony'; Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'irony'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Irony' (browser, 2026-09-05) for verbal/situational/dramatic categories; Grokipedia 'Ironic (song)' for the Alanis Morissette 1995 examples. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: verify the three-category classification is standard in Fowler before writing T4.
framing_note: Punchline via misuse: T2 rain on a wedding. Cultural anchor T3: the Alanis song is grade-10-safe and famous enough that many parents will recognize the lesson. Vocab-teaching T1 defines IRONIC inline. Distractor pool: unfortunate/coincidental/sarcastic/paradoxical -- close-but-wrong labels.

name: Less vs fewer: uncountable vs countable
scope: The rule the supermarkets ignore. T1: the canonical punchline -- '10 ITEMS OR LESS' on the express-lane sign is technically wrong; items can be COUNTED (one, two, three) so it should be '10 items or FEWER'. T2: define the rule inline -- FEWER goes with things you can COUNT (fewer cookies, fewer people, fewer cars); LESS goes with things you MEASURE as a mass (less water, less flour, less time). T3: the memory trick -- if you can put a NUMBER in front of the noun, use FEWER; if you cannot, use LESS. Fewer three cookies (yes, count); less three water (no, measured). T4: the judgment traps -- MONEY, TIME, DISTANCE, and WEIGHT are usually treated as MASS even though we count units of them: 'less than $10', 'less than five minutes', 'less than three miles', 'less than 20 pounds'. Because we treat the amount as a single measured quantity, LESS is standard. T5: identify which sentence is correct in FORMAL writing -- 'fewer than three items', 'less than three miles', 'fewer than ten dollars' (this one is wrong: money is treated as mass; should be LESS), 'less water in the glass' (correct).
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.250 (less vs fewer); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'less, fewer'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Fewer vs less' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the money/time/distance mass-treatment exception and the '10 items or less' supermarket example.
framing_note: Punchline via a real-world sign every kid has seen. Vocab-teaching T2 defines COUNTABLE vs MASS inline. Distractor pool: other count/mass errors, other supermarket-sign errors ('express lain' misspelling, misplaced apostrophe).

name: Nauseous vs nauseated: the strict distinction
scope: The word that flipped meaning in modern speech. T1: the strict meaning -- NAUSEOUS means 'causing nausea' (a nauseous smell makes you feel sick); NAUSEATED means 'feeling nausea' (I am nauseated after the roller coaster). T2: the punchline via misuse -- 'I feel nauseous' -- taken strictly, this means the SPEAKER is causing nausea in others (the speaker is the stinky thing), not that they feel sick. T3: the modern-usage reality -- since the mid-1900s, 'nauseous' has been used to mean both, and dictionaries now list both senses; in casual speech 'I feel nauseous' is understood and standard. T4: the register call -- in FORMAL medical writing, keep NAUSEOUS = causing and NAUSEATED = feeling; in casual conversation, either is understood. Which sentence would a careful copy editor prefer? T5: identify which uses the strict sense correctly -- 'the nauseous smell of spoiled milk' (strict: the smell CAUSES nausea, correct), 'the child was nauseated by the boat ride' (strict: the child FEELS nausea, correct), 'I feel nauseous' (strict-wrong / casual-OK).
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'nauseous, nauseated'; Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'nauseous'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Nauseous' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the strict-vs-modern distinction and the dual-sense dictionary listings.
framing_note: PRESCRIPTIVE-DESCRIPTIVE case: teach the strict distinction as formal-writing preference while noting the casual usage is standard. Punchline via misuse T2. Vocab-teaching T1 defines both terms inline with example. Distractor pool: other confusable pairs (sick/ill, dizzy/faint).

name: May vs might: permission and possibility
scope: Two closely-related modal verbs with a subtle split. T1: the two main uses of MAY -- permission ('May I be excused?') and possibility ('It may rain tomorrow'). MIGHT is used mostly for possibility, usually a WEAKER or more remote possibility ('It might snow in July -- unlikely but possible'). T2: the punchline via ambiguity -- 'You may not go to the party' could mean 'you are not allowed' (permission denied) OR 'it is possible you will not' (possibility). Context disambiguates, but the double meaning is a real trap. T3: the tense clue -- MIGHT is the historical past tense of MAY, and in reported speech it usually replaces MAY: 'She said she MAY come' -> 'She said she MIGHT come'. T4: the strict-vs-modern split -- traditionalists prefer MIGHT for hypothetical/counterfactual possibility ('If we had left earlier, we MIGHT have caught the train'); using MAY here ('we MAY have caught') sounds like the possibility is still open, but the train has already left. T5: identify which uses the strict distinction -- 'You may leave the table' (permission, correct), 'It might rain tonight -- 30 percent chance' (weak possibility, correct), 'If she had studied, she may have passed' (traditionalist-wrong: should be MIGHT for counterfactual).
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'may, might'; Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'may and might'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'English modal verbs' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the permission-vs-possibility split and the counterfactual MIGHT rule.
framing_note: Punchline via T2 ambiguity. Vocab-teaching T1 defines both uses inline. Distractor pool: other modal verbs (can, could, shall, should, will, would).

name: Can vs may: ability vs permission
scope: The classroom classic. T1: the strict distinction -- CAN asks about ABILITY ('Can I lift this rock?' = am I strong enough?); MAY asks about PERMISSION ('May I lift this rock?' = am I allowed?). T2: the punchline via the teacher's joke -- Student: 'Can I go to the bathroom?' Teacher: 'I don't know -- CAN you?' The teacher is pointing out that CAN asks whether the student is physically able, not whether the student has permission. T3: the modern-usage reality -- in casual speech CAN is used for both ability AND permission ('Can I have a cookie?'), and this has been standard in informal English since the late 1800s. Formal writing and polite requests still prefer MAY. T4: the register call -- in a job interview, at a formal dinner, or in a business letter, 'May I' is more polite; among friends 'Can I' is normal. Which sentence fits the register? T5: identify which uses the strict distinction -- 'Can she reach the top shelf?' (ability, correct), 'May I borrow your pencil?' (permission, formal-correct), 'Can I leave now?' (permission, casual-OK / formal-loose).
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'can, may'; Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'can'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'English modal verbs' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the ability-vs-permission distinction.
framing_note: Punchline via the classic teacher joke at T2. Vocab-teaching T1 defines both uses. Distractor pool: other modals (might, could, would).

name: Shall vs will: the nearly-extinct distinction
scope: A rule most Americans have never heard of. T1: the historical British-English rule -- for plain future statements, use SHALL with I and WE ('I shall arrive tomorrow'), and WILL with you/he/she/they ('you will arrive tomorrow'). T2: for EMPHASIS or determination, reverse it -- 'I WILL arrive tomorrow' (determined), 'you SHALL arrive tomorrow' (a command or promise). This is why the Fairy Godmother in Cinderella says 'You shall go to the ball' -- a promise, not just a future statement. T3: the extinction in American English -- since the mid-1900s Americans use WILL for almost all futures; SHALL survives mostly in legal writing ('the tenant shall pay rent') and in a few formal fixed phrases ('shall we dance?'). T4: the legal-writing survival -- in contracts, SHALL means 'is required to' (a mandatory duty), and lawyers still debate whether every SHALL should be replaced with MUST or WILL to avoid ambiguity. T5: identify which uses the traditional British rule -- 'I shall see you tomorrow' (British-future, correct), 'You shall not pass!' (emphasis/command, correct -- Gandalf on the bridge), 'We will overcome' (American-standard future, correct in modern usage).
source: PRIMARY: Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'shall and will'; Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'shall, will'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Shall and will' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the historical British rule, the American extinction, and the legal-writing survival.
framing_note: Punchline via T2's Cinderella promise ('you shall go to the ball'). Vocab-teaching T1 lays out the rule inline. Distractor pool: other modals (may, might, must, should).

name: Who vs whom: the he/him substitution trick
scope: The pronoun most kids give up on. T1: the punchline via misuse -- 'Whom is at the door?' sounds wrong (and IS wrong: the person at the door is the SUBJECT of the sentence, so it should be WHO). T2: define the categories inline -- WHO is a SUBJECT pronoun (does the action); WHOM is an OBJECT pronoun (receives the action). Compare: 'HE went to the store' (subject) vs 'I saw HIM at the store' (object). T3: the he/him substitution trick -- rearrange the sentence to a statement and try HE or HIM: 'Who did you invite?' -> 'You invited HIM' (him works, so WHOM is technically correct: 'Whom did you invite?'). 'Who is at the door?' -> 'HE is at the door' (he works, so WHO is correct). T4: the register call -- in FORMAL writing (essays, business letters), use WHOM correctly; in casual speech, WHO is now standard for both roles ('Who did you invite?' is understood by everyone). Fowler noted the decline of WHOM as early as 1926. T5: identify which uses WHOM correctly in formal writing -- 'To whom it may concern' (object of TO, correct), 'Whom shall I say is calling?' (WRONG -- WHO is the subject of 'is calling'; a famous over-correction trap), 'Who wrote this?' (WHO is subject, correct).
source: PRIMARY: Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'who, whom'; Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'who, whom'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Who (pronoun)' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the he/him substitution trick and the WHOM-decline history.
framing_note: PRESCRIPTIVE-DESCRIPTIVE case: teach the strict distinction as a formal-writing marker while acknowledging WHO is now standard in speech. Punchline via T5's over-correction trap ('Whom shall I say is calling?'). Vocab-teaching T2 defines SUBJECT vs OBJECT pronouns inline. Distractor pool: other case errors (I/me, he/him, we/us).

name: Different from, different than, different to
scope: Three prepositions, one comparison. T1: the American-English preference -- DIFFERENT FROM is the most widely-accepted form in formal writing on both sides of the Atlantic ('cats are different FROM dogs'). T2: DIFFERENT THAN is common in American English, especially when introducing a clause ('the movie was different than I expected'). Some strict traditionalists dislike it, but Merriam-Webster and most modern usage guides accept it. T3: DIFFERENT TO is standard in British English ('cats are different TO dogs'). Americans rarely use it; the British rarely use DIFFERENT THAN. T4: the register call -- in formal American writing, DIFFERENT FROM is the safe choice; DIFFERENT THAN is standard in speech and journalism; DIFFERENT TO marks the writer as British. Which fits the register? T5: identify which is standard in FORMAL American English -- 'different from what I expected' (safe, correct), 'different than what I expected' (American-informal-OK), 'different to what I expected' (British, out-of-register for an American essay).
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'different'; Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'different from, than, to'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Different from' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the US/UK preposition split and the modern acceptance of DIFFERENT THAN.
framing_note: Punchline via the three-way split. Register-and-clarity contrast. Distractor pool: other British-vs-American usage splits (color/colour, math/maths, in hospital/in the hospital).

name: Compared to vs compared with
scope: A subtle distinction most writers ignore. T1: the strict distinction -- COMPARED TO is used to point out a LIKENESS between things of DIFFERENT categories ('Shakespeare compared a summer's day TO his beloved -- summer and a person are different kinds of things'). T2: COMPARED WITH is used for a POINT-BY-POINT examination between things of the SAME category ('cats compared WITH dogs -- both are pets'). T3: the punchline via a famous line -- Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 begins 'Shall I compare thee TO a summer's day?' -- the speaker is drawing an analogy across categories (person vs day), so TO is correct. If Shakespeare had been listing feature-by-feature ('you are warmer than a summer's day, brighter than a summer's day'), WITH would fit. T4: the modern reality -- most style guides note the distinction, but few writers observe it consistently; both forms are now used interchangeably in casual writing. Formal scientific writing usually prefers COMPARED WITH for statistical comparisons ('the treated group compared WITH the control group'). T5: identify which uses the strict distinction -- 'compared her singing to a bird's' (analogy across categories, correct), 'compared the two candidates with each other' (point-by-point within a category, correct), 'compared apples with oranges' (traditional idiom, actually a mixed case).
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'compared to, compared with'; Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'compare'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sonnet 18' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the 'shall I compare thee to a summer's day' anchor.
framing_note: Punchline via T3's Sonnet 18 anchor -- a beloved literary line that shows the strict rule in action. Vocab-teaching T1-T2 defines both uses inline with example. Distractor pool: other prepositional distinctions (in/on, at/by, from/of).

name: Between vs among: two vs more than two
scope: The strict count-based split. T1: the strict rule -- BETWEEN is used for TWO things ('choose between the red door and the blue door'); AMONG is used for THREE OR MORE things ('choose among the ten flavors of ice cream'). T2: the punchline via misuse -- 'the treasure was divided AMONG the two pirates' sounds off; two pirates should share BETWEEN them. T3: the exception that trips people up -- BETWEEN is correct for more than two things when the relationships are ONE-TO-ONE, individually considered ('a treaty between the five nations' -- each nation has a distinct relationship with each other; AMONG would suggest a single group blur). T4: the register call -- in formal writing, observe the count-based rule; 'between three friends' is technically correct if the friends have individual pairwise relationships (each friend shares secrets with each other friend), but 'among three friends' is safer if the group is being treated as one blur. T5: identify which is correct in FORMAL writing -- 'between you and me' (two people, correct -- and note that BETWEEN takes object pronouns: never 'between you and I'), 'among the crowd' (crowd is many, correct), 'between the twelve jurors' (twelve people acting as individual pairs discussing evidence, correct under the exception).
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.250; Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'between, among'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Between vs among' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the count-based rule and the individually-considered exception.
framing_note: Punchline via T2 misuse. Vocab-teaching T1 lays out the rule inline. Bonus T5 rung catches the 'between you and I' hypercorrection (BETWEEN is a preposition, takes object case). Distractor pool: other count-vs-mass distinctions (less/fewer, much/many, amount/number).

name: If I was vs if I were: the subjunctive mood
scope: The one place English still uses the subjunctive. T1: the canonical punchline -- Tevye's song from Fiddler on the Roof begins 'If I WERE a rich man' -- not 'if I was'. WERE is the SUBJUNCTIVE form, used for HYPOTHETICAL or CONTRARY-TO-FACT statements. Tevye is NOT rich; the sentence describes a wish that is not true. T2: define SUBJUNCTIVE inline -- a special verb form for wishes, hypotheticals, and things contrary to fact ('if I were you', 'I wish I were taller', 'she acts as if she were the queen'). T3: the rule -- use WERE with I/he/she/it when the IF-clause describes a situation that is UNTRUE or UNLIKELY. Compare 'If I WAS late yesterday, I apologize' (past fact, possibly true -- indicative WAS) vs 'If I WERE late every day, they would fire me' (hypothetical, contrary to fact -- subjunctive WERE). T4: the modern-usage reality -- in casual speech, 'if I was' is now common even for hypotheticals; formal writing still prefers WERE. Some style guides call the subjunctive 'dying'; it survives strongest in fixed phrases ('if I were you', 'as it were'). T5: identify which uses the subjunctive correctly -- 'If I were king, I would abolish homework' (hypothetical, correct), 'If she was here yesterday, I did not see her' (possible past fact, correct indicative), 'I wish I was taller' (formal-wrong: WERE for wishes).
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.128 (subjunctive mood); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'subjunctive'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'English subjunctive' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the survival in fixed phrases and the Fiddler on the Roof anchor.
framing_note: PRESCRIPTIVE-DESCRIPTIVE case for T5's 'wish I was'. Punchline via Tevye's song T1. Vocab-teaching T2 defines SUBJUNCTIVE inline with multiple examples. Distractor pool: other mood forms (indicative, imperative, conditional).

name: Farther vs further: distance vs metaphor
scope: A useful split most writers observe. T1: the strict distinction -- FARTHER refers to PHYSICAL distance ('the store is farther down the road'); FURTHER refers to METAPHORICAL or figurative distance, or means 'additional' ('let us discuss this further', 'no further questions'). T2: the punchline via misuse -- 'we need to look FURTHER down the road for the store' works only if you mean the metaphorical road; for the actual road, FARTHER is precise. T3: the memory trick -- FARTHER has FAR in it (physical distance you can measure); FURTHER has FUR-, no distance clue. When in doubt, if you can substitute 'more distant' physically, use FARTHER. T4: the FURTHER-as-additional sense -- 'furthermore', 'without further ado', 'no further comment', 'further education' -- FARTHER cannot replace FURTHER in any of these; the split is only in the distance sense. T5: identify which is precise in formal writing -- 'the moon is farther from Earth than any object we have visited' (physical distance, correct), 'we need to investigate this further' (metaphorical/additional, correct), 'she read further into the book' (pages progressed, metaphorical -- FURTHER preferred, though FARTHER is defensible).
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'farther, further'; Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'farther, further'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Farther' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the physical-vs-metaphorical distinction and the FUR-has-no-distance mnemonic.
framing_note: Punchline via T2 misuse. Vocab-teaching T1 defines both inline. Distractor pool: other confusable pairs (fewer/less, among/between).

name: Active vs passive voice: when the actor matters
scope: The single biggest concision lesson. T1: define ACTIVE VOICE inline -- the SUBJECT does the action ('The child kicked the ball'). Define PASSIVE VOICE inline -- the subject RECEIVES the action, and the actor may be hidden or moved to the end ('The ball was kicked' or 'The ball was kicked by the child'). T2: the punchline via responsibility-hiding -- 'MISTAKES WERE MADE' is the classic passive dodge; it is grammatical, but it hides WHO made the mistakes. Compare the active 'THE MANAGER MADE MISTAKES' -- named, direct, accountable. T3: when PASSIVE is the RIGHT choice -- when the actor is unknown ('the window was broken overnight'), when the actor is irrelevant ('the vaccine was developed in 2020'), or in scientific reporting where the RESULT matters more than the researcher ('the sample was heated to 100 degrees'). Passive is a TOOL, not a sin. T4: the concision test -- active sentences are usually shorter and stronger. 'The report was written by the intern' (7 words, passive) vs 'The intern wrote the report' (5 words, active). Which reads faster? T5: identify which uses ACTIVE voice -- 'the dog chased the mailman' (active, subject does the action, correct), 'the mailman was chased by the dog' (passive, subject receives), 'errors were made in the report' (passive, actor hidden), 'the accountant made errors in the report' (active, actor named).
source: PRIMARY: Strunk and White, The Elements of Style, rule 14 ('Use the active voice'); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'passive voice'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Passive voice' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the 'mistakes were made' dodge and the legitimate scientific-passive uses.
framing_note: Punchline via T2's famous passive dodge. Vocab-teaching T1 defines ACTIVE and PASSIVE inline. IMPORTANT: T3 legitimizes passive rather than banning it (moral-vision-adjacent: no fabricated rules). Distractor pool: other voice/mood distinctions (indicative, subjunctive).

name: Concision: eliminating deadwood phrases
scope: Strunk and White's central lesson. T1: the canonical deadwood -- 'DUE TO THE FACT THAT' should be BECAUSE. 'AT THIS POINT IN TIME' should be NOW. 'IN THE EVENT THAT' should be IF. Every short version says the same thing in fewer words. T2: the punchline via bloat -- 'at this point in time, due to the fact that the meeting has been cancelled, we will be in a position to reschedule for a future date' (28 words) vs 'the meeting was cancelled; we can reschedule' (7 words). Same meaning, one-quarter the length. T3: the standard deadwood list -- 'FOR ALL INTENTS AND PURPOSES' (drop entirely or 'essentially'), 'IN ORDER TO' (just TO), 'THE QUESTION AS TO WHETHER' (WHETHER), 'IS OF THE OPINION THAT' (BELIEVES or THINKS), 'IT SHOULD BE NOTED THAT' (drop entirely). T4: the Strunk rule -- his famous line: 'Omit needless words. Vigorous writing is concise.' From The Elements of Style, 1918. Applied ruthlessly, it cuts many published sentences in half. T5: identify which sentence is the most concise revision -- given a bloated original ('at this point in time, we are of the opinion that further discussion would be beneficial'), pick the tightest correct rewrite ('we should discuss this further' or 'let us discuss').
source: PRIMARY: Strunk and White, The Elements of Style, rule 17 ('Omit needless words'); Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.220 (concision). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'The Elements of Style' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the 1918 Strunk-alone edition and the 'omit needless words' rule anchor.
framing_note: Punchline via T2's 28-to-7-word cut. Anchor T4 to Strunk 1918. Distractor pool: other writing sins (passive voice, weasel words, cliches).

name: Verb tense consistency: do not jump tenses mid-paragraph
scope: The most common paragraph-level error. T1: the canonical punchline -- 'I walked to the store, and then I BUY some milk' -- the first verb is past tense (WALKED), the second is present (BUY); pick one and stick with it. Correct: 'I walked to the store, and then I BOUGHT some milk'. T2: the rule -- within a paragraph or a single narrative sequence, keep verb tenses CONSISTENT unless the meaning genuinely shifts (a flashback, a general truth). T3: the legitimate tense-shift -- 'Yesterday I visited the museum (past). It IS the largest in the city (present -- still true).' The shift here is meaningful: the visit is past, but the museum's size is a general present fact. T4: the HISTORICAL PRESENT trap -- writers sometimes tell past-tense stories in the present ('Napoleon MARCHES on Moscow') for immediacy; once you start, stay in it, do not slip back to past mid-scene ('Napoleon MARCHES on Moscow, and his army SUFFERED'). T5: identify which paragraph is tense-consistent -- given four short paragraphs, pick the one that keeps its tenses aligned throughout.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.126 (tense sequence); Strunk and White, The Elements of Style, rule 12 (use verbs of consistent tense). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sequence of tenses' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the historical-present convention.
framing_note: Punchline via T1 tense-jump. T3 legitimizes the meaningful shift. Distractor pool: other verb errors (agreement, mood, voice).

name: Verb mood: indicative, imperative, subjunctive, conditional
scope: The four moods of English verbs. T1: define MOOD inline -- the FORM a verb takes to show whether the speaker is stating a fact, giving a command, wishing, or supposing. The four moods in English are indicative, imperative, subjunctive, and conditional. T2: INDICATIVE -- states a fact or asks a question ('the sun rises in the east', 'is it raining?'). This is the workhorse mood; most sentences are indicative. T3: IMPERATIVE -- gives a command or request; the subject 'you' is usually understood, not spoken ('close the door', 'please pass the salt', 'do not touch that'). T4: SUBJUNCTIVE -- expresses a wish, a hypothetical, or a contrary-to-fact statement ('I wish I WERE taller', 'if I WERE king', 'she demanded that he BE present' -- note the bare BE). Rare in modern English but still standard in fixed phrases. T5: CONDITIONAL -- expresses what WOULD happen under certain conditions, often paired with an IF-clause ('if it rained, I WOULD stay home'). Identify which mood a given sentence uses.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition sections 5.126-5.130 (verb moods); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'mood'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Grammatical mood' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the four-mood taxonomy in English.
framing_note: Category-teaching ladder at T2-T5 with example sentences for each mood. Vocab-teaching T1 defines MOOD inline. Distractor pool: other verb properties (tense, voice, aspect). Note: MOOD is category-naming (voice hierarchy #4) so stays at T3-T5, taught by example.

name: Second person and imperatives in instructions
scope: The right voice for instructions. T1: the canonical punchline -- 'ONE SHOULD TAKE THE BOX AND CARRY IT TO THE KITCHEN' is stiff and awkward; 'TAKE THE BOX TO THE KITCHEN' (imperative, YOU understood) is direct and natural. T2: the rule for how-to writing -- use the IMPERATIVE mood, addressed to the reader as YOU. Recipe books, assembly instructions, and user manuals all use imperatives: 'preheat the oven', 'insert tab A into slot B', 'click the save button'. T3: why the stiff form fails -- 'one should' and 'the user must' put distance between the writer and the reader; imperatives cut through that. Compare a recipe: 'One should combine the flour and the sugar' vs 'combine the flour and the sugar' -- the second reads like a friend at your elbow. T4: the register call -- FORMAL academic and legal writing sometimes avoids imperatives ('the applicant should complete section 3'); everyday instructional writing (recipes, manuals, tutorials) uses them. Which fits the register? T5: identify which is the better instructional form -- 'take the box to the kitchen' (imperative, direct), 'one should take the box to the kitchen' (stiff third-person), 'the box should be taken to the kitchen' (passive, actor missing).
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.211 (imperative mood in instructions); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'imperative'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Imperative mood' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the second-person-implied convention.
framing_note: Register-contrast ladder. Vocab-teaching T2 defines IMPERATIVE inline with examples. Distractor pool: other formal-vs-casual register choices.

name: Register: casual, formal, academic, technical, literary
scope: The five main registers of English. T1: define REGISTER inline -- the LEVEL OF FORMALITY a writer or speaker chooses to fit the audience and occasion. A text to a friend is not written the same way as a job application. T2: CASUAL register -- contractions, slang, short sentences, informal address ('hey, wanna grab lunch?'). Used in texts, chats, notes between friends. T3: FORMAL register -- full words, no slang, courteous distance ('Dear Ms. Smith, I would like to inquire about the position advertised on Monday'). Used in business letters, job applications, formal invitations. T4: ACADEMIC register -- precise vocabulary, cited sources, third-person voice ('this paper examines the relationship between X and Y'). Used in essays, research papers, textbooks. TECHNICAL register -- specialized vocabulary for a specific field ('the compiler flags a segmentation fault at line 47'). Used in manuals, specifications, engineering documents. T5: LITERARY register -- inventive vocabulary, figurative language, rhythm, imagery ('the fog crept in on little cat feet' -- Sandburg 1916). Used in poetry, novels, essays as art. Identify which register fits a given passage.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.220 (register); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'register'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Register (sociolinguistics)' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the five-register taxonomy and the Sandburg 'Fog' 1916 literary anchor.
framing_note: Category-teaching ladder. Vocab-teaching T1 defines REGISTER inline. Anchor T5 to Sandburg's 'Fog' (1916), a widely-taught safe literary example. Distractor pool: other stylistic distinctions (voice, tone, mood).

name: Contractions in formal writing
scope: A simple register marker. T1: the rule -- in FORMAL academic writing, expand contractions: DON'T becomes DO NOT, CAN'T becomes CANNOT, IT'S becomes IT IS, WE'LL becomes WE WILL. Contractions signal casual register; formal writing avoids them. T2: the punchline via mismatch -- imagine a job cover letter that begins 'Hi, I'm super excited about this job -- it'd be great to work with y'all' -- the contractions and slang shout CASUAL when the occasion calls for FORMAL. T3: the exceptions -- contractions are FINE (even preferred) in dialogue, in personal essays, in journalism, in blog posts, and in most modern nonfiction that aims for a conversational voice. The rule against them applies mainly to academic papers, legal writing, and formal correspondence. T4: the register-check test -- read your writing aloud. If it sounds like a person talking to a friend, contractions belong. If it sounds like a lecture or a legal brief, expand them. T5: identify which sentence fits FORMAL academic register -- 'The results do not support the hypothesis' (expanded, correct), 'The results don't support the hypothesis' (casual-OK, academic-out), 'It's clear that further research is needed' (casual-OK, academic-expand to 'It is clear').
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.104 (contractions); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'contractions'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Contraction (grammar)' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the register-marking convention.
framing_note: Punchline via T2's cover-letter mismatch. Register-clarity contrast. Distractor pool: other formality markers (slang, informal address, sentence fragments).

name: Sentence variety and rhythm
scope: The Gary Provost lesson. T1: the canonical exhortation -- writer Gary Provost's famous demonstration paragraph shows the problem and the fix: strings of same-length sentences read monotonously ('I write with short sentences. And I write with medium sentences. And sometimes long sentences'), while VARIED lengths create rhythm and hold attention. T2: the rule -- mix SHORT sentences (punchy, memorable), MEDIUM sentences (the main workhorse), and OCCASIONAL LONG sentences (for detail, complexity, or building momentum). The variety itself carries the reader forward. T3: Strunk and White's related rule (rule 14) -- vary the beginnings of sentences; if every sentence in a paragraph starts with THE or I, the paragraph reads flat. Start some sentences with a phrase, a clause, a conjunction. T4: the pacing effect -- a SHORT sentence after several long ones LANDS. Notice how this rung has three long sentences and then this one. Snap. T5: identify which paragraph has genuine sentence variety -- given four short paragraphs, pick the one that mixes sentence lengths rather than repeating one length.
source: PRIMARY: Strunk and White, The Elements of Style, rule 14 (use varied sentence structure); Gary Provost, 100 Ways to Improve Your Writing (1985) -- the famous variety-demonstration paragraph. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Gary Provost' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the writing-teacher lineage and the demonstration-paragraph anchor.
framing_note: Category-and-rhythm ladder. Anchor T1 to Provost's demonstration and T3 to Strunk 1918. T4 demonstrates the effect within the rung itself. Distractor pool: other stylistic virtues (concision, clarity, voice).

name: Redundancy: ATM machine, PIN number, advance planning
scope: The most common form of wordiness. T1: the canonical punchline -- 'ATM MACHINE' is redundant; ATM stands for AUTOMATIC TELLER MACHINE, so 'ATM machine' is 'Automatic Teller Machine machine'. Same with PIN NUMBER (Personal Identification Number number) and VIN NUMBER (Vehicle Identification Number number). T2: define REDUNDANCY inline -- using two or more words that mean the SAME thing, so one repeats the other. Redundancy adds length without adding information. T3: the standard redundancy list -- 'ADVANCE PLANNING' (planning is always in advance), 'CLOSE PROXIMITY' (proximity means closeness), 'END RESULT' (results come at the end), 'FREE GIFT' (gifts are free), 'FUTURE PLANS' (plans are for the future), 'PAST HISTORY' (history is by definition past), 'PERSONALLY I THINK' (thinking is personal). T4: the acronym redundancy trap -- 'HIV VIRUS' (Human Immunodeficiency Virus virus), 'LCD DISPLAY' (Liquid Crystal Display display), 'RAS SYNDROME' -- 'Redundant Acronym Syndrome syndrome', a jokey name for the phenomenon itself. T5: identify which phrase is redundant -- 'PIN number' (redundant, PIN is Number), 'my personal opinion' (redundant, opinions are personal), 'seven a.m. in the morning' (redundant, a.m. means morning), 'the tallest building in the city' (not redundant).
source: PRIMARY: Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'redundancy, tautology'; Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'redundancy'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'RAS syndrome' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the acronym-redundancy meta-joke and the ATM/PIN/HIV list.
framing_note: Punchline via T1 acronym-expansion. Vocab-teaching T2 defines REDUNDANCY inline. T4's RAS syndrome is the meta-joke every kid should meet. Distractor pool: other wordiness sins (deadwood phrases, weak modifiers, cliches).

name: Dead metaphors and cliches: think outside the box
scope: Overused phrases that signal lazy writing. T1: the canonical worn-out list -- 'THINK OUTSIDE THE BOX', 'AT THE END OF THE DAY', 'LOW-HANGING FRUIT', 'MOVE THE NEEDLE', 'CIRCLE BACK', 'TOUCH BASE'. Each was once vivid; each is now business-speak wallpaper. T2: define CLICHE inline -- a phrase that was once original and striking, but has been repeated so often it has lost its force; the reader skims past it without seeing an image. T3: define DEAD METAPHOR inline -- a metaphor that has been used so often it no longer registers as figurative. 'The FOOT of the bed' is a dead metaphor (a bed does not have literal feet); most speakers do not even notice the image. Dead metaphors are usually harmless; cliches are usually not. T4: the George Orwell rule -- from his 1946 essay 'Politics and the English Language': 'Never use a metaphor, simile, or other figure of speech which you are used to seeing in print.' Freshness matters. T5: identify which sentence uses a cliche -- 'let us think outside the box on this' (cliche, business-speak), 'her argument was a house of cards' (fresh metaphor, image intact), 'at the end of the day, it comes down to hard work' (cliche opener), 'the runner sprinted like a hunted deer' (fresh simile).
source: PRIMARY: George Orwell, 'Politics and the English Language' (1946); Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'cliche'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Cliche' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the standard corporate-speak list and Orwell's rules.
framing_note: Punchline via T1's business-speak list. Vocab-teaching T2-T3 defines CLICHE and DEAD METAPHOR inline (they are NOT the same thing). Anchor T4 to Orwell 1946. Distractor pool: other freshness sins (jargon, buzzwords, empty intensifiers).

name: Text-speak vs formal register: LOL, IMO, IIRC
scope: The clearest modern register violation. T1: the canonical mismatch -- imagine a history essay that begins 'LOL, so basically the American Revolution happened bc the British were, IMO, taxing them WAY too much, IIRC'. The text-speak abbreviations and slang belong in a text message, not an academic essay. T2: define TEXT-SPEAK inline -- the abbreviations and informal spellings developed for phone texting and chat: LOL (laughing out loud), IMO (in my opinion), IIRC (if I recall correctly), BTW (by the way), TBH (to be honest), IDK (I don't know), FWIW (for what it's worth). T3: the register call -- text-speak is standard in texts, chat messages, and casual social posts. It is OUT in formal essays, business letters, job applications, and academic writing. Using it in the wrong register makes the writer look careless or unaware of the audience. T4: the emoji problem -- emojis (smiley faces, thumbs up, hearts) are similarly casual-register; a smiley face in a business report signals informality. Formal writing avoids them; casual writing uses them freely. T5: identify which sentence fits FORMAL academic register -- 'The results were, IMO, inconclusive' (text-speak, out), 'The results were inconclusive' (formal, correct), 'lol the experiment failed' (text-speak, out), 'The experiment did not produce the expected results' (formal, correct).
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'informal English'; Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.220 (register). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'SMS language' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the standard text-speak abbreviation list.
framing_note: Punchline via T1's history-essay mismatch. Register-clarity contrast. Vocab-teaching T2 defines the abbreviations inline (kids may recognize some, not others). Distractor pool: other casual-register markers (contractions, slang, emojis).
